subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. Be a Storyteller. It is a unit about repetition — the way stories and songs, and computer programs, do the same thing again and again. You become storytellers who notice that a good story is full of repeats, and then you learn how a computer handles a repeat neatly using a loop. Think of how many stories work: a character knocks three times, three travellers ask the same question, a song's chorus comes back after every verse. In our own day we repeat actions too, like stirring a pot round and round. Repetition is everywhere — and that is the big idea of this unit. In computing we give it a name: iteration. First, a loop is a set of instructions that is repeated. Second, one single pass through those instructions is called an iteration — so if a loop runs four times, there are four iterations. Third, a counter keeps track of how many times the loop has run, and a loop that repeats a set, known number of times is called a count-controlled loop. Fourth, you learn to use repetition to make a long algorithm shorter, and then to build it in Scratch with the Repeat block.

outcomes: Explain that a loop is a set of instructions that is repeated, and give an example from a story or a song.
Understand that an iteration is one single pass through the repeated steps, and count the iterations in an algorithm.
Understand that a counter keeps track of how many times a loop has run.
Recognise a count-controlled loop — a loop that repeats a set (known) number of times.
Use repetition to make a long algorithm shorter, keeping the same result.
Follow and correct an algorithm that uses repetition (put a jumbled story back in order).
In Scratch, build a program using the Repeat block (a count-controlled loop) and change the counter number.

concepts.title: Stories that repeat: loops and iterations
concepts.explanation: A loop is a set of instructions that is repeated. When we go through those instructions one time, that is one iteration. If the loop runs several times, there are several iterations. Start with a story — storytellers already know all about repeats. Tell it slowly, counting the repeats on your fingers.

concepts.title: The counter and the count-controlled loop
concepts.explanation:
A counter keeps track of how many times a loop has run. When we know the exact number of times to repeat, we can write the loop in a short way and say “repeat these steps N times”. A loop that repeats a set, known number of times is called a count-controlled loop. This makes a long algorithm much shorter.

concepts.title: Into Scratch: the Repeat block
concepts.explanation: The same idea works on the computer. In Scratch, the Repeat block is a count-controlled loop. It is a C-shaped block from the Control group: you drop the steps you want to repeat inside its mouth, and you type the counter number at the top. First build the LONG way — the repeated blocks written out four times — and run it with the green flag Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu, click Create, and keep the Cat sprite (it has two costumes, so it looks like it is walking). Choose a simple backdrop like Blue Sky. Tell you our storyteller cat is going to walk across to greet a friend, taking four steps.
concepts.example: Find one real example of into Scratch: the Repeat block around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drop the repeated blocks INSIDE the C-shape (not underneath it)? Can you change the counter number and predict what will happen? Can you find the repeat ( ) block in the Control group?

concepts.title: A loop that draws: the square
concepts.explanation:
A count-controlled loop can draw a shape. To draw a square you do the same two steps four times: move forward, then turn a right-angle (90 degrees). This is a perfect four-iteration count-controlled loop, and it makes a lovely picture for a story scene (a window, a picture frame, a floor tile).

First show the idea unplugged.

concepts.title: Tell your repeating story (put it together)
concepts.explanation: You build a short Scratch story where a count-controlled loop does the repeating part. Changing the counter number changes how many times the repeat happens — so the storyteller is in control. Long ago, on a clear night, Nora looked up and counted the stars. Add the Star sprite and a night backdrop (like Stars or Night City), make sure the Pen extension is on (for the stamp block), and build this together
